questions.q: The word 'environment' is derived from the French word 'environner'. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Environment comes from the French 'environner', meaning to encircle or surround. It refers to everything that surrounds a living organism.
why_wrong: Environner does not mean to protect.
It has no sense of producing anything.
It has no sense of consuming anything.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the environment?
options: Only the plants and animals of a forest, according to some views
Only human-made structures in a city, under usual conditions
Only the climate of a region, as is often assumed
The sum total of all living and non-living things around an organism
questions.explain: The environment is the total of biotic and abiotic surroundings that influence an organism. It is not limited to one part such as climate or forests.
why_wrong: This leaves out non-living components such as air, water and soil.
Environment includes natural surroundings too, not just built ones.
Climate is just one part of the environment.

questions.q: Who coined the term 'ecology' in 1866?
questions.explain: Ernst Haeckel, a German biologist, coined 'oekologie' in 1866. It is the study of relationships between organisms and their surroundings.
why_wrong: Darwin is known for natural selection, not for coining ecology.
Suess is credited with the term biosphere.
Carson wrote Silent Spring much later, in 1962.

questions.q: In which year was the Environment (Protection) Act enacted in India?
questions.explain: The Environment (Protection) Act was passed in 1986, after the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984. It is the umbrella law for environmental protection in India.
why_wrong: 1972 was the Stockholm Conference, and the Wildlife Protection Act year, not the EPA.
1992 was the Rio Earth Summit year.
The Biological Diversity Act came in 2002, not the EPA.

questions.q: On which date is World Environment Day observed every year?
questions.explain: World Environment Day is observed on 5 June, as started by the UN after the 1972 Stockholm Conference. It aims to encourage awareness and action for the environment.
why_wrong: This is Earth Day.
This is World Ozone Day.
This is World Water Day.

questions.q: The UN Conference on the Human Environment, the first major global environment conference, was held in which city in 1972?
questions.explain: The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment took place in Stockholm, Sweden. It led to the creation of UNEP and to World Environment Day.
why_wrong: Rio hosted the Earth Summit in 1992.
Kyoto is linked to the 1997 climate protocol.
Paris is linked to the 2015 climate agreement.

questions.q: The study of the interaction between living organisms and their physical surroundings is called what?
questions.explain: Ecology deals with the relationship between organisms and their environment. It is the basic science underlying environmental studies.
why_wrong: Geology studies the Earth's solid structure and rocks.
Meteorology studies weather and the atmosphere.
Anthropology studies human societies and cultures.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NATURAL part of the environment rather than a human-made one?
questions.explain: Rivers exist without human construction and are part of the natural environment. Highways, dams and power plants belong to the built environment.
why_wrong: A highway is built by humans.
A dam is a human-made structure.
A power plant is a human-made structure.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches an environmental event with its year?
options: Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro - 1992
questions.explain: The Earth Summit (UNCED) was held in Rio in 1992, and gave Agenda 21. The other pairs mix up the years.
why_wrong: Stockholm was held in 1972.
Bhopal happened in 1984.
The EPA was enacted in 1986.

questions.q: Which statement correctly separates 'environment' from 'ecology'?
options: They are exactly the same thing with different spellings, according to some views
Ecology is the surroundings; environment is the science of studying them, under usual conditions
Environment refers only to humans; ecology refers only to plants, as is often assumed
Environment is the surroundings; ecology is the study of how organisms relate to those surroundings
questions.explain: Environment is what surrounds an organism, while ecology is the science of the interactions between organisms and that surrounding. Mixing them up is a common error.
why_wrong: One is the surroundings, the other is a branch of science.
This reverses the two definitions.
Both terms cover all organisms, not just one group.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT an example of the 'built' or man-made environment?
questions.explain: A coral reef is a natural ecosystem formed by living coral polyps. Railways, skyscrapers and canals are products of human construction.
why_wrong: Railways are constructed by people.
Skyscrapers are human-built.
Irrigation canals are dug by people.

questions.q: The Environment (Protection) Act of 1986 was passed in India mainly in the aftermath of which event?
questions.explain: The Bhopal gas leak of December 1984 exposed the lack of a strong environmental law. The EPA 1986 was enacted to provide one under Article 253 of the Constitution.
why_wrong: Chernobyl happened in Ukraine, not India.
Chipko was a forest-protection movement of the 1970s.
That was a conservation movement, not the trigger for this Act.

questions.q: Living components of the environment, such as plants and animals, are called what?
questions.explain: Biotic components include all living organisms: plants, animals and microbes. Non-living parts such as air, water and soil are abiotic.
why_wrong: Abiotic means non-living.
Physical is not the standard term for living parts.
This refers to non-living substances.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic component of the environment?
questions.explain: Sunlight is a non-living physical factor, so it is abiotic. Bacteria, fungi and earthworms are all biotic.
why_wrong: Bacteria are living organisms.
Fungi are living organisms.
Earthworms are living animals.

questions.q: Green plants are called producers because they do what?
options: They absorb food made by animals
questions.explain: Producers (autotrophs) prepare food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. All other organisms depend on them directly or indirectly.
why_wrong: That describes consumers.
That is the role of decomposers.
Plants make their own food.

questions.q: Organisms that break down dead plants and animals into simple substances are called what?
questions.explain: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil. This completes nutrient cycling.
why_wrong: Producers make food by photosynthesis.
They eat plants.
They eat other animals.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a primary consumer?
questions.explain: Primary consumers are herbivores that feed directly on producers. A grasshopper eating leaves fits this role.
why_wrong: A lion is a secondary or tertiary consumer.
A mushroom is a decomposer.
Grass is a producer.

questions.q: Temperature, light, water and soil are examples of which type of factors?
questions.explain: Temperature, light, water and soil are non-living physical factors, so they are called abiotic. They determine which organisms can live in a place.
why_wrong: Biotic means living.
Trophic relates to feeding levels.
These relate to inheritance.

questions.q: Which of the following is an energy source for almost all ecosystems on Earth?
questions.explain: The Sun supplies the energy that producers capture through photosynthesis. Nearly all food chains begin with this solar energy.
why_wrong: The Moon does not supply usable energy to ecosystems.
Wind itself is driven by solar heating.
Soil holds nutrients but is not the primary energy source.

questions.q: Which of the following lists contains ONLY abiotic components?
questions.explain: Air, rock, rainfall and temperature are all non-living. Each of the other lists contains an organism such as fungi, bacteria or algae.
why_wrong: Fungi are living.
Bacteria are living.
Algae are living.

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out among these ecosystem components?
questions.explain: A mushroom is a fungus and a decomposer, whereas wheat, mango and grass are producers. This makes it the odd one out.
why_wrong: Wheat is a producer.
A mango tree is a producer.
Grass is a producer.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the role of decomposers in the environment?
options: They are the main source of energy for the ecosystem
They recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil
They only feed on living plants
They convert sunlight into chemical energy
questions.explain: Decomposers release nutrients locked in dead organisms so that producers can use them again. Without them, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter.
why_wrong: Energy comes from the Sun through producers.
Decomposers act on dead organic matter.
This is photosynthesis, done by producers.

questions.q: Which is a correct match of a component to its type?
questions.explain: Humidity is a non-living atmospheric factor. Earthworms and algae are living and therefore biotic.
why_wrong: Earthworms are living, so they are biotic.
Soil moisture is non-living.
Algae are living, so they are biotic.

questions.q: Which of the following is correctly classified as a heterotroph?
questions.explain: Heterotrophs depend on other organisms for food, and a cow feeds on plants. The others are autotrophs that perform photosynthesis.
why_wrong: Rice makes its own food.
Cyanobacteria photosynthesise, so they are autotrophs.
Spirogyra is a photosynthetic alga.

questions.q: In which respect do abiotic components differ from biotic ones?
options: They are non-living factors that influence living organisms
They are all capable of reproduction, in most situations
They are produced by decomposers only, according to some views
They always form the food chain, under usual conditions
questions.explain: Abiotic components are non-living and set the conditions for life, such as light, water and minerals. They do not reproduce or form the food chain.
why_wrong: Only living things reproduce.
Abiotic factors are not produced by decomposers.
Food chains consist of living organisms.

questions.q: Which sphere of the Earth consists of rocks, soil and minerals?
questions.explain: The lithosphere is the solid outer shell of the Earth, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It holds rocks, soil and minerals.
why_wrong: The hydrosphere is made of water.
The atmosphere is the layer of gases.
The biosphere is the zone of life.

questions.q: The hydrosphere includes which of the following?
options: Only the water in living cells
questions.explain: The hydrosphere is the total water of the Earth in liquid, solid and vapour forms. It covers oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater and glaciers.
why_wrong: It also includes rivers, lakes, groundwater and ice.
Rain is just one part of the water cycle.
It covers all water on Earth, not just within organisms.

questions.q: The envelope of gases surrounding the Earth is called what?
questions.explain: The atmosphere is the blanket of gases held around the Earth by gravity. It supplies air, protects from harmful radiation and moderates temperature.
why_wrong: This is the rocky part.
This is the water part.
This is the living part.

questions.q: The zone of the Earth where life exists is called what?
questions.explain: The biosphere is the part of the Earth where living organisms are found. It overlaps the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.
why_wrong: This is a layer of the atmosphere.
This is the solid part of the Earth.
This is the outermost layer of the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which gas makes up the largest portion of dry air in the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Nitrogen forms roughly 78 percent of dry air, with oxygen at about 21 percent. The rest is argon, carbon dioxide and other trace gases.
why_wrong: Oxygen is second, at about 21 percent.
Carbon dioxide is only a trace gas.
Argon is present in under 1 percent.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does most weather occur?
questions.explain: The troposphere is the lowest layer, holding most of the air's mass and water vapour. Clouds, rain and storms occur there.
why_wrong: This holds the ozone layer and has little weather.
This is a higher, cold layer where meteors burn up.
This is a very high layer with auroras and satellites.

questions.q: The ozone layer is found in which layer of the atmosphere?
questions.explain: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere and absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. It protects life on the surface.
why_wrong: This is the lowest layer, where weather occurs.
This is above the stratosphere.
This is the outermost layer.

questions.q: Which statement about the water of the hydrosphere is correct?
options: Most of Earth's water is fresh and found in rivers, in most situations
Most fresh water is stored in the atmosphere, according to some views
Most of Earth's water is in lakes, under usual conditions
Most water is saline ocean water; most fresh water is in ice and glaciers
questions.explain: About 97 percent of the water is saline ocean water. Of the small fresh water share, most is stored as ice caps and glaciers.
why_wrong: Rivers hold a tiny fraction of the total.
The atmosphere holds very little water.
Lakes hold only a small share.

questions.q: Arrange the atmospheric layers from the ground upwards.
questions.explain: The layers rise as troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, then the exosphere. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere.
why_wrong: Troposphere is the lowest layer, not the second.
Stratosphere comes before the mesosphere.
This lists them from the top down.

questions.q: Which of these is a part of the lithosphere?
questions.explain: Soil is formed from weathered rock and belongs to the lithosphere. Water bodies fall under the hydrosphere and gases under the atmosphere.
why_wrong: Ocean water belongs to the hydrosphere.
Ozone belongs to the atmosphere.
Water vapour belongs to the atmosphere.

questions.q: Why is the biosphere often described as an overlap zone rather than a separate layer?
options: Because it lies entirely above the atmosphere, as is often assumed
Because it contains no non-living matter, in most situations
Life exists in parts of the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere
Because it is composed only of the oceans, according to some views
questions.explain: Living organisms are found in soil, water and air, so the biosphere spans portions of all three spheres. It is where the realms interact.
why_wrong: The biosphere is not above the atmosphere.
It involves non-living matter too, as organisms depend on it.
It covers land and air as well as water.

questions.q: Match the sphere to its main content: which pairing is correct?
options: Atmosphere - gases such as nitrogen and oxygen
Hydrosphere - rocks and minerals, in most situations
Lithosphere - clouds and winds, according to some views
Biosphere - the ozone layer, under usual conditions
questions.explain: The atmosphere is made of gases such as nitrogen and oxygen. Rocks go with the lithosphere and living things with the biosphere.
why_wrong: Rocks belong to the lithosphere.
Clouds and winds belong to the atmosphere.
Ozone is part of the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a layer of the atmosphere?
questions.explain: The asthenosphere is a part of the Earth's upper mantle below the lithosphere. Mesosphere, stratosphere and exosphere are atmospheric layers.
why_wrong: This is a layer of the atmosphere.
This is a layer of the atmosphere.
This is a layer of the atmosphere.

questions.q: Rain falling and filling a river is an interaction between which two spheres?
questions.explain: Water vapour condenses in the atmosphere and falls as rain into the hydrosphere. This is one part of the water cycle linking the realms.
why_wrong: Rain originates from atmosphere and ends in water bodies.
Neither of these starts the process.
These are layers of the same sphere, not two spheres.

questions.q: The word 'biosphere' was first introduced by which scientist?
questions.explain: The Austrian geologist Eduard Suess introduced the term biosphere in 1875. Vladimir Vernadsky later developed the concept.
why_wrong: Haeckel coined 'ecology'.
Elton is known for work on food chains and niches.
Leopold is known for land ethic ideas.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Environmental studies is described as multidisciplinary because it does what?
options: It is taught in only one department, in most situations
It draws on many subjects, such as biology and economics
It deals only with plants, according to some views
It ignores social sciences, under usual conditions
questions.explain: Environmental problems have physical, biological and social aspects, so the subject uses many disciplines together. This is what multidisciplinary means.
why_wrong: This contradicts multidisciplinarity.
It covers far more than plants.
It includes social science and economics.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: What is the main aim of environmental awareness?
options: To increase industrial output, according to some views
To discourage the use of science, under usual conditions
To create concern and encourage responsible action
To promote the use of more resources, as is often assumed
questions.explain: Awareness helps people understand the environment and act responsibly. It underpins sustainable use of resources.
why_wrong: This is not the aim of awareness.
Science is used in solving environmental problems.
Awareness promotes careful use.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which subject is MOST directly linked with studying pollutants and their reactions in air and water?
questions.explain: Chemistry helps to understand pollutants and their reactions. It is one of the contributing disciplines of environmental studies.
why_wrong: History does not analyse pollutants.
Music has no link with pollutant analysis.
Literature does not analyse pollutants.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which of the following is a scope of environmental studies?
questions.explain: The scope includes natural resources and their conservation, ecosystems, biodiversity and pollution. It also includes social issues related to the environment.
why_wrong: This is not a scope of EVS.
This is unrelated.
This is unrelated.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which of these is an important reason for studying environmental studies?
questions.explain: Environmental studies helps us see the impact of human actions on land, water and air. It guides us to make sustainable choices.
why_wrong: EVS is science-based.
EVS aims to reduce waste.
EVS teaches careful use of resources.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which pairing of discipline and its contribution to environmental studies is correct?
options: Economics - valuing resources and costs of environmental damage
Geology - studying human laws, according to some views
Sociology - studying atmospheric layers, under usual conditions
Mathematics - classifying plants, as is often assumed
questions.explain: Economics helps in valuing resources and weighing the costs of environmental damage. Geology studies the Earth's materials and sociology studies society.
why_wrong: Law is not studied in geology.
Atmospheric layers belong to physical sciences.
Plant classification belongs to botany.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: A town plans a new factory. Which discipline helps predict the effect of its waste water on local fish?
questions.explain: Ecology explains effects on organisms and chemistry explains the pollutants. This shows why the subject needs many disciplines.
why_wrong: Astronomy does not address this.
Linguistics does not address this.
Music theory does not address this.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an objective of environmental education?
options: Building skills to solve environmental problems
Encouraging participation in protecting the environment
Increasing the exploitation of natural resources without limit
questions.explain: Environmental education aims at awareness, knowledge, attitude, skills and participation. Unlimited exploitation of resources goes against its aims.
why_wrong: Awareness is a key objective.
Skills are an objective.
Participation is an objective.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which statement shows the importance of environmental studies for engineers?
options: It helps design projects that cause less harm to the environment
It removes the need for safety rules, in most situations
It makes technology unnecessary, according to some views
It only concerns forest officers, under usual conditions
questions.explain: Engineers shape industry, buildings and infrastructure, so EVS helps them reduce impact. It is relevant across professions.
why_wrong: It supports rules, not removes them.
It does not reject technology.
It concerns every profession.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: The multidisciplinary nature of environmental studies is BEST shown by which example?
options: Air pollution needs chemistry, health science, law and economics
Air pollution needs only physics, according to some views
Air pollution concerns only lawyers, under usual conditions
Air pollution is studied only in geography, as is often assumed
questions.explain: Air pollution has chemical causes, health effects, legal controls and economic costs. Several disciplines are needed together.
why_wrong: It needs far more than one subject.
Many fields are involved.
Geography alone is not enough.

questions.topic: Scope and importance of environmental studies
questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about the scope of environmental studies?
options: It covers only wildlife photography, under usual conditions
It covers only industrial design, as is often assumed
It covers only space research, in most situations
It covers natural resources, ecosystems, biodiversity and pollution
questions.explain: The scope covers natural resources, ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution control and related social issues. It is broad and multi-field.
why_wrong: Its scope is much wider.
Its scope is wider.
It is not about space research.

questions.q: What is sustainability?
options: Using all resources quickly for present benefit, as is often assumed
Meeting present needs without harming the needs of future generations
Stopping all human development, in most situations
Depending only on non-renewable resources, according to some views
questions.explain: Sustainability balances present needs with those of future generations. It follows the Brundtland definition of sustainable development.
why_wrong: This ignores future needs.
Sustainability does not mean stopping development.
Non-renewable resources run out.

questions.q: Which report, published in 1987, popularised the idea of sustainable development?
questions.explain: Our Common Future, by the Brundtland Commission, defined sustainable development in 1987. It is the standard source of the definition.
why_wrong: Silent Spring (1962) was about pesticides.
That was published in 1972 by the Club of Rome.
This was an action plan adopted in 1992.

questions.q: The three pillars of sustainability are environmental, economic and what else?
questions.explain: The standard pillars are environment, economy and society. They are often shown as overlapping circles.
why_wrong: Technology is not one of the three pillars.
This is not the standard third pillar.
This is not the standard third pillar.

questions.q: The 'triple bottom line' refers to which three Ps?
questions.explain: The triple bottom line measures social (people), environmental (planet) and economic (profit) performance. It mirrors the three pillars.
why_wrong: These are not the three Ps.
These are not the three Ps.
These are marketing Ps, not the triple bottom line.

questions.q: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
questions.explain: Solar energy is renewable because it is continually available. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable.
why_wrong: Coal takes millions of years to form.
Petroleum is a fossil fuel.
Natural gas is a fossil fuel.

questions.q: The economic pillar of sustainability is mainly concerned with what?
questions.explain: The economic pillar means growth that supports livelihoods and can continue over time. It must not damage the environment or society.
why_wrong: This is not an economic aim.
This is not an aim.
This is not an aim.

questions.q: Which of the following actions mainly supports the SOCIAL pillar of sustainability?
options: Planting trees on a barren hill
Raising the profit of a company
questions.explain: The social pillar deals with equity, health, education and wellbeing. Tree planting and solar panels are environmental, and company profit is economic.
why_wrong: This mainly supports the environmental pillar.
This mainly supports the economic pillar.
This mainly supports the environmental pillar.

questions.q: A development project makes high profit but destroys a forest and displaces villagers. Which statement is correct?
options: It fails sustainability because it ignores environmental and social pillars
It is fully sustainable because profit is high, under usual conditions
It is sustainable since the economy grows, as is often assumed
Sustainability does not apply to projects, in most situations
questions.explain: Sustainable development needs balance among economy, environment and society. A project that satisfies only the economic pillar is not sustainable.
why_wrong: Sustainability needs all three pillars.
Economic growth alone is not enough.
It applies to all development.

questions.q: Which statement distinguishes renewable from non-renewable resources correctly?
options: Renewable resources can never be used up under any use, as is often assumed
Non-renewable resources form quickly, in most situations
Renewables are replenished naturally in human time; non-renewables are not
Both types regenerate at the same rate, according to some views
questions.explain: Renewables like wind, sunlight and forests regenerate naturally, though overuse can deplete some. Non-renewables such as coal form over geological time.
why_wrong: Overuse can still deplete them, such as forests or fish.
They take millions of years.
Their rates differ greatly.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT a feature of sustainable development?
options: Fairness between present and future generations
Conservation of natural resources for later use
Maintaining the balance of ecosystems and nature
questions.explain: Sustainable development takes the future into account. Using resources with no regard for future generations is the opposite.
why_wrong: Intergenerational equity is a core feature.
Conservation is a core feature.
This is a core feature.

questions.q: Which pairing of pillar and example is correct?
options: Environmental pillar - protecting biodiversity and reducing pollution
Economic pillar - protecting wetlands, according to some views
Social pillar - extracting more coal, under usual conditions
Environmental pillar - increasing company dividends, as is often assumed
questions.explain: Protecting biodiversity and controlling pollution belongs to the environmental pillar. Dividends belong to the economic pillar.
why_wrong: Wetland protection is an environmental aim.
Coal extraction is not a social aim.
Dividends are economic.

questions.q: What is meant by 'intergenerational equity'?
options: Equal wages for all workers today, under usual conditions
Equal rainfall in all regions, as is often assumed
Fairness between present and future generations
Equal population in all countries, in most situations
questions.explain: Intergenerational equity means present generations should leave the environment in a condition that allows future ones to meet their needs. It underlies the Brundtland definition.
why_wrong: This is about current economic fairness.
This has nothing to do with the concept.
This has nothing to do with the concept.

questions.q: Which of these is a sustainable practice for managing a forest?
options: Clear-felling the whole forest at once
Burning the forest for quick farmland
Selling all timber in one year
questions.explain: Sustainable yield means harvesting no more than the forest can regenerate. Replanting keeps the resource available for the future.
why_wrong: This destroys the resource.
This causes loss of habitat and soil.
This does not allow regrowth.

questions.q: What does 'carrying capacity' mean?
options: The total weight a truck can carry
The minimum number of organisms in an area
The number of species on Earth
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the largest population of a species that an environment can sustain without being degraded. It is set by the availability of resources.
why_wrong: This is not the ecological meaning.
It is a maximum, not a minimum.
This is a biodiversity measure.

questions.q: Carrying capacity is usually denoted by which letter?
questions.explain: In population models, K stands for carrying capacity. In the logistic growth curve, growth levels off at K.
why_wrong: Lowercase r is used for growth rate in some models.
N is the population size.
T is not the symbol for carrying capacity.

questions.q: Which of the following can limit the carrying capacity of an area?
questions.explain: Food, water, space and other resources limit how many individuals can survive. These are the limiting factors that set K.
why_wrong: This is not a limit by itself.
This has no effect.
This is not a direct limit on resources.

questions.q: What happens if a population exceeds the carrying capacity of its environment?
questions.explain: Beyond K, resources are used faster than they regenerate. This causes starvation and decline of the population.
why_wrong: The environment does not grow.
They become scarce instead.
It usually crashes after overshoot.

questions.q: The S-shaped growth curve of a population levels off near which value?
questions.explain: In logistic growth, the population rises and then levels near K. This forms the S-shaped curve.
why_wrong: Birth rate is a rate, not the limit.
Death rate is a rate, not the limit.
Population does not level off at zero.

questions.q: Which of these is a limiting factor for a deer population in a forest?
questions.explain: Food shortage reduces the number of deer the forest can support. Limiting factors set the carrying capacity.
why_wrong: This is not limiting.
This is unrelated.
This is not limiting.

questions.q: Which statement about the carrying capacity of an ecosystem is correct?
options: It can change if resources or conditions change
It is fixed forever for every species
It depends only on birth rate
It is the same for all species in an area
questions.explain: Carrying capacity depends on resource supply, climate and technology, so it can rise or fall. A drought, for example, lowers it.
why_wrong: It changes with conditions.
Resource availability matters too.
It differs between species.

questions.q: A pasture can sustain 100 cattle. A farmer puts 250 on it. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Overgrazing and degradation of the pasture
questions.explain: Exceeding capacity leads to overgrazing and soil damage. The pasture may then support fewer animals than before.
why_wrong: Overgrazing does not speed growth.
Resources will be depleted.
The land gets degraded and capacity may fall.

questions.q: Which factor is most likely to RAISE the carrying capacity for humans in an area?
questions.explain: Better farming and irrigation increase food output, supporting more people. Drought, erosion and water loss reduce it.
why_wrong: This lowers capacity.
This lowers capacity.
This lowers capacity.

questions.q: Ecological footprint is best described as what?
options: Land and water area needed to support one person's lifestyle
The number of footprints left on a trail, according to some views
The number of species in a forest, under usual conditions
The weight of a person, as is often assumed
questions.explain: The ecological footprint measures human demand on nature. It is compared with the planet's biocapacity to judge sustainability.
why_wrong: This is not the ecological concept.
This is biodiversity.
This is unrelated.

questions.q: If an island's food supply is halved by a cyclone, what happens to its carrying capacity for a deer population?
questions.explain: Carrying capacity depends on resources, so reduced food lowers it. The deer population will tend to decline to match it.
why_wrong: Food halved reduces capacity.
Capacity depends on food supply.
No environment has infinite capacity.

questions.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted by the United Nations?
questions.explain: The UN adopted 17 SDGs in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda. They replaced the 8 Millennium Development Goals.
why_wrong: Eight was the number of Millennium Development Goals.
The UN adopted more than 12.
There are not 20 goals.

questions.q: By which year are the SDGs meant to be achieved?
questions.explain: The SDGs are part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The target year is 2030.
why_wrong: The target is later than this.
The target is later than this.
The target is earlier than this.

questions.q: SDG 1 aims at which of the following?
questions.explain: SDG 1 is 'No Poverty', which seeks to end poverty everywhere. Zero hunger is SDG 2.
why_wrong: This is SDG 2.
This is SDG 4.
This is SDG 13.

questions.q: Which SDG is about clean water and sanitation?
questions.explain: SDG 6 deals with clean water and sanitation for all. Energy is SDG 7 and climate action is SDG 13.
why_wrong: SDG 4 is quality education.
SDG 7 is affordable and clean energy.
SDG 13 is climate action.

questions.q: SDG 13 is concerned with which theme?
questions.explain: SDG 13 calls for urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts. Life below water is SDG 14.
why_wrong: This is SDG 14.
This is SDG 5.
This is SDG 2.

questions.q: The SDGs were adopted by the UN General Assembly in which year?
questions.explain: The UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Agenda and its 17 SDGs in September 2015.
why_wrong: This is the Rio Earth Summit year.
The Millennium Development Goals were set around 2000.
This is much later than the adoption.

questions.q: Which SDG focuses on 'Life on Land'?
questions.explain: SDG 15 aims to protect and restore terrestrial ecosystems, forests and biodiversity. SDG 14 covers life below water.
why_wrong: SDG 14 is life below water.
SDG 12 is responsible consumption and production.
SDG 11 is sustainable cities and communities.

questions.q: Which pairing of SDG number and theme is correct?
options: SDG 12 - life on land and forests
questions.explain: SDG 7 stands for affordable and clean energy. The other options mismatch numbers and themes.
why_wrong: Education is SDG 4.
Climate action is SDG 13.
Life on land is SDG 15.

questions.q: Which SDG is concerned with responsible consumption and production?
questions.explain: SDG 12 promotes sustainable consumption and production patterns, including waste reduction. SDG 9 relates to industry and infrastructure.
why_wrong: SDG 9 is industry, innovation and infrastructure.
SDG 10 is reduced inequalities.
SDG 16 is peace, justice and strong institutions.

questions.q: The SDGs replaced which earlier set of global goals?
questions.explain: The SDGs followed the 8 Millennium Development Goals, which ran to 2015. The SDGs are broader and cover environmental issues more fully.
why_wrong: Kyoto set emission targets, not development goals.
Agenda 21 was an earlier action plan.
Montreal concerns ozone-depleting substances.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT one of the 17 SDG themes?
questions.explain: Gender equality (5), reduced inequalities (10) and partnerships for the goals (17) are SDGs. A ban on travel is not a goal.
why_wrong: This is SDG 5.
This is SDG 10.
This is SDG 17.

questions.q: A village builds a solar mini-grid for homes and a school. Which SDG is MOST directly served?
questions.explain: A solar mini-grid provides clean energy, directly serving SDG 7. It may help other goals indirectly.
why_wrong: The project does not address marine life.
It does not directly address food supply.
It does not directly address institutions or justice.

questions.q: Which SDG is most closely linked to protecting oceans and marine resources?
questions.explain: SDG 14 is 'Life Below Water', which concerns conservation of oceans, seas and marine resources.
why_wrong: SDG 6 is clean water and sanitation.
SDG 13 is climate action.
SDG 15 is life on land.

questions.q: Which statement about the SDGs is correct?
options: They are universal, applying to all countries, and are integrated and indivisible
They apply only to developing countries, in most situations
They deal only with environmental issues, according to some views
They are legally binding treaties with penalties, under usual conditions
questions.explain: The SDGs apply to every nation and link economic, social and environmental concerns. They are not legally binding.
why_wrong: They apply to all countries.
They cover social and economic goals too.
They are voluntary goals, not binding treaties.

questions.q: Match the SDG to its theme: which is correct?
questions.explain: SDG 2 is zero hunger, whereas SDG 1 is no poverty and SDG 4 is quality education.
why_wrong: No poverty is SDG 1.
Quality education is SDG 4.
Gender equality is SDG 5.

questions.q: A town planner describes the 'environment' of her city as the lake, the factory, the slum and the temple festival crowd together. Which view of environment does this reflect?
options: Only the untouched natural surroundings in most cases
Only the living organisms of an area in most cases
questions.explain: Environment is the total of everything that surrounds and influences an organism, so it is not limited to nature alone.
why_wrong: A factory and a slum are human-made, so excluding them narrows environment wrongly.
Living things are just the biotic part; surroundings also include non-living and human-made elements.
These are physical components only and leave out biological and social dimensions.

questions.q: A factory discharges effluent into a river, fish die, and farmers downstream lose yield. Which idea about the environment does this chain best show?
options: Each component of the environment works in isolation
Only human activities form part of the environment
Disturbance in one part spreads to others
Water pollution affects only the aquatic organisms
questions.explain: Components of the environment are interconnected, so pollution of water affects organisms and then human livelihoods.
why_wrong: If components were isolated, downstream farmers would not be affected.
The river, fish and soil are natural parts too, so this is incorrect.
Irrigation with polluted water also hurts crops, so effects are not confined to fish.

questions.q: Which statement correctly separates 'environment' from 'ecosystem'?
options: Ecosystem is a functional system; environment is the surroundings
They are exact synonyms with no difference
Environment contains only biotic parts and ecosystem only abiotic parts
Ecosystem is limited to one species' habitat while environment covers the whole biosphere
questions.explain: Environment refers to the external conditions around an organism, whereas an ecosystem is the interacting system of living and non-living parts with energy flow and nutrient cycling.
why_wrong: They differ in scope: one is surroundings, the other a functional system.
Both involve living and non-living parts; neither is restricted to one type.
An ecosystem involves many species and can be any scale, so this reverses the idea.

questions.q: A village replaces mud huts and open fields with concrete houses, roads and a power plant. Which type of environment has expanded?
questions.explain: Houses, roads and power plants are constructed by humans, forming the built or human-made environment.
why_wrong: Natural environment consists of features not created by people, such as forests and rivers.
Concrete structures are non-living, so they are not biotic.
Roads and buildings are not part of the air envelope.

questions.q: The term 'ecology' was coined in 1866 by a German biologist. Who was he, and what does the Greek root 'oikos' mean?
options: Charles Elton; the study of nature
questions.explain: Ernst Haeckel coined 'ecology' from the Greek oikos (house/home) and logos (study), meaning study of organisms in their home.
why_wrong: Elton was a later ecologist, and oikos means house, not study.
Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in 1935, and oikos does not mean energy.
Odum wrote on ecosystem ecology but did not coin the term, and oikos is not water.

questions.q: A surveyor listing features of a coastal district sorts them into natural and human-made. Which item belongs to the human-made group?
options: An irrigation canal cut across the delta
A mangrove swamp at the river mouth under normal conditions
The monsoon wind from the sea under normal conditions
questions.explain: A canal is constructed by people, whereas the other features occur without human construction.
why_wrong: Mangroves grow naturally, so they are part of the natural environment.
Wind is an atmospheric phenomenon, not human-made.
Reefs are built by living corals, so they are natural.

questions.q: Which description matches the legal definition of environment in India's Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?
options: Only air, water and land as physical media, excluding living beings
Water, air, land and their links with living things and property
Only the flora and fauna of notified protected forests
Only natural resources used for commercial purposes
questions.explain: The Act defines environment broadly as water, air and land plus the inter-relationship between them and all living beings and property.
why_wrong: The Act explicitly includes living creatures, plants and micro-organisms and their inter-relationships.
The definition is not limited to protected forests or to biological components.
The Act does not restrict environment to commercially used resources.

questions.q: A delayed monsoon raises vegetable prices in city markets and forces farmers to sow late. This shows that
options: nature influences social and economic systems
social systems operate independently of nature
questions.explain: Rainfall is a natural factor, and its change affects agriculture, markets and household budgets.
why_wrong: The price rise shows dependence on rainfall, not independence.
The monsoon is a natural factor that clearly altered prices.
Here rainfall influenced the economy, not the reverse.

questions.q: In a paddy field an ecologist notes Azolla, dissolved oxygen, frogs, soil pH and sunlight. How many of these are abiotic factors?
questions.explain: Dissolved oxygen, soil pH and sunlight are non-living, while Azolla (a plant) and frogs are living.
why_wrong: A third non-living item remains: dissolved oxygen, soil pH and sunlight are all abiotic.
Azolla and frogs are living, so only three items are abiotic.
Two of the five are living organisms, so not all are abiotic.

questions.q: A botanist records soil pH, soil texture, rainfall and wind speed. Which two are edaphic factors?
questions.explain: Edaphic factors relate to soil, so pH and texture qualify; rainfall and wind are climatic.
why_wrong: These are climatic factors, not soil factors.
Rainfall is climatic, so this pair mixes types.
Wind speed is climatic, so this pair mixes types.

questions.q: After a week of heavy cloud, algae in a village pond release much less oxygen. Which abiotic component is limiting?
options: Light, the energy source for photosynthesis
The number of herbivores for the most part as a general rule
Pond bed rock type for the most part as a general rule
questions.explain: Reduced sunlight lowers photosynthesis, which lowers oxygen output by algae.
why_wrong: Soil texture does not control photosynthetic oxygen release in a pond within a week.
Herbivores are biotic, and the cause here is the cloud cover.
Rock type does not change with cloud cover.

questions.q: In a grassland food chain of grass, grasshopper, frog, snake and hawk, which statement is correct?
options: The grasshopper is a secondary consumer
The hawk is a tertiary consumer
The snake is a tertiary consumer
The frog is a primary consumer
questions.explain: Grasshopper is primary, frog secondary, snake tertiary and hawk quaternary consumer.
why_wrong: It feeds on grass, a producer, so it is a primary consumer.
The hawk is one level beyond the snake, making it a quaternary consumer.
The frog eats grasshoppers, so it is a secondary consumer.

questions.q: Cow dung dropped in a field is gradually broken down and its nutrients return to the soil. Which group is mainly responsible?
options: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria
Primary consumers such as grasshoppers in most cases
Tertiary consumers such as snakes in most cases
questions.explain: Decomposers break down dead and waste organic matter and release nutrients for producers.
why_wrong: Producers make food by photosynthesis and do not break down dung.
Primary consumers eat plants, not dung decomposition products as a main role.
Predators feed on animals and do not recycle dung nutrients.

questions.q: An algal bloom depletes dissolved oxygen in a lake and fish die. Which description of the components involved is accurate?
options: Only abiotic components interacted under normal conditions for the most part
No component interacted; it was a random event under normal conditions
Biotic change altered an abiotic factor, which hit other biotic life
questions.explain: Algae (biotic) lowered oxygen (abiotic) and the fish (biotic) suffered, showing interactions among components.
why_wrong: Algae and fish are living, so biotic components were involved.
Dissolved oxygen is an abiotic factor that carried the effect.
The sequence shows linked cause and effect among components.

questions.q: A meteorologist records humidity, temperature, wind and precipitation at a hill station. These belong to which group of factors?
questions.explain: They are non-living atmospheric conditions that together describe climate.
why_wrong: Edaphic means soil-related and these are neither biotic nor soil factors.
Biotic means living, and these are non-living.
They are not about land shape and are not living.

questions.q: Earthworms and fungi both act on dead matter. Which statement distinguishes them correctly?
options: Earthworms ingest and fragment detritus; fungi digest it externally
Both are producers that fix carbon
Fungi ingest detritus and earthworms digest it externally as a general rule
Earthworms are decomposers and fungi are detritivores as a general rule
questions.explain: Detritivores swallow organic debris; decomposers secrete enzymes outside the body and absorb the products.
why_wrong: Neither is a producer; both feed on organic matter.
This reverses their modes of feeding.
The labels are swapped.

questions.q: A geologist explains that India's tectonic plate is a rigid slab moving over a softer layer. The slab corresponds to which realm?
options: The asthenosphere in most cases under normal conditions
The troposphere in most cases under normal conditions
The lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle)
questions.explain: Tectonic plates are pieces of the lithosphere, which rides over the weaker asthenosphere.
why_wrong: This is the weaker layer beneath the plates, not the plate itself.
This is the lowest layer of the atmosphere.
This is a liquid layer deep inside the Earth, not a plate.

questions.q: Which statement about the lithosphere is correct?
options: It consists of the crust only
Crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle
It includes the whole mantle down to the outer core
It is the gaseous envelope above the crust
questions.explain: The lithosphere is the strong outer shell of Earth including crust and top mantle.
why_wrong: It also includes the rigid uppermost mantle.
Only the top rigid part of the mantle is included.
That describes the atmosphere.

questions.q: Rain and lichens slowly break a granite outcrop in the Western Ghats into soil. What does this show about Earth's realms?
options: All four realms interact in soil formation
The realms are completely independent for the most part
Only the lithosphere is involved for the most part
Only the biosphere acts on rock
questions.explain: Rock (lithosphere), water, air and organisms jointly drive weathering.
why_wrong: Weathering needs inputs from several realms.
Rain and lichens are from other realms.
Water and air also weather rock.

questions.q: A seismologist notes an abrupt change in seismic wave speed at the Mohorovicic discontinuity. Which two layers does it separate?
questions.explain: The Moho is the boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle below.
why_wrong: That boundary is the Gutenberg discontinuity.
That boundary is the Lehmann discontinuity.
The Moho is inside the solid Earth, not at the surface.

questions.q: Villages below a Himalayan glacier depend on its melt. Which store holds the largest share of Earth's fresh water, of which this glacier is a tiny part?
questions.explain: Most fresh water is locked in polar ice caps and glaciers rather than lakes, rivers or groundwater.
why_wrong: These hold only a very small fraction of fresh water.
It is large but smaller than the ice store.
It is a tiny fraction of fresh water.

questions.q: A student claims most of Earth's water is fresh and easily usable. Which correction is accurate?
options: About 97 percent of the hydrosphere is fresh river water under normal conditions
Oceans hold only about 10 percent of Earth's water under normal conditions
Groundwater makes up most of the hydrosphere
About 97 percent of the hydrosphere is saline ocean water
questions.explain: Most water is saline, and most of the small fresh share is frozen, so little is readily usable.
why_wrong: Rivers hold a tiny share and most water is saline.
Oceans hold the vast majority.
Groundwater is a small share compared to oceans.

questions.q: Rain falls on a field, soaks into the soil surface, and later reaches the water table. Which processes occur in order?
questions.explain: Water first enters the soil surface (infiltration) and then moves downward through soil and rock (percolation).
why_wrong: Runoff is flow over the surface, which does not describe soaking in.
These involve water going into the air, not downward.
This reverses the correct order.

questions.q: Farmers in Punjab pump borewells faster than the monsoon refills them. Which hydrosphere store is being depleted?
options: Atmospheric vapour as a general rule
Ocean surface water as a general rule
questions.explain: Borewells draw from groundwater, and extraction beyond recharge lowers the water table.
why_wrong: Borewells do not tap polar ice.
Pumping does not remove water vapour from the air.
Borewells draw from aquifers, not the open ocean.

questions.q: A pilot climbs above storm clouds to a smoother cruising altitude. In which layer do clouds and storms normally occur?
questions.explain: Weather such as clouds, rain and storms occurs in the lowest layer, the troposphere.
why_wrong: This layer lies above and is relatively calm.
This layer is far higher and has no usual weather.
This is very high and contains the ionosphere, not clouds.

questions.q: A news report on thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica refers to ozone mainly located in which layer?
questions.explain: The ozone layer is concentrated in the stratosphere, where it absorbs harmful UV radiation.
why_wrong: Ozone here is a pollutant, not the protective layer.
Ozone is minimal at this height.
This is the outermost layer and has no ozone layer.

questions.q: Temperature rises with height in the stratosphere. What is the main reason?
options: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and releases heat
It is closer to the heat of the Earth's surface for the most part
Meteors burn there continuously for the most part as a general rule
questions.explain: Absorption of UV by ozone heats the upper stratosphere.
why_wrong: The troposphere is closer to the surface, and the stratosphere is farther.
Meteors burn mostly in the mesosphere and do not explain the trend.
Clouds are in the troposphere.

questions.q: A student says that air is mostly oxygen. Which correction about dry air by volume is right?
options: Oxygen is about 78 percent and nitrogen about 21 percent as a general rule
Carbon dioxide is about 78 percent as a general rule in most cases
Nitrogen is about 78 percent and oxygen about 21 percent
questions.explain: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas, followed by oxygen at roughly one fifth.
why_wrong: The values are swapped.
CO2 is a trace gas.
Argon is under 1 percent.

questions.q: The ionosphere, which reflects radio waves, is mainly located in which layer?
questions.explain: Ionisation by solar radiation produces charged particles in the thermosphere that reflect radio waves.
why_wrong: Weather occurs here, not the ionosphere.
Ozone is dominant here.
The ionosphere does not mainly lie in this outermost layer.

questions.q: Bacteria thrive at deep-sea vents and birds fly several kilometres above ground. What does this show about the biosphere?
options: It is a separate layer apart from other realms under normal conditions
It is limited to land surfaces
A thin zone overlapping the other three realms
It is the same as the atmosphere under normal conditions
questions.explain: Life exists wherever conditions allow across the other three realms.
why_wrong: It overlaps the others.
Life exists in water and air as well.
The biosphere includes more than the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which statement about the biosphere is NOT true?
options: It is the zone of Earth where life exists
It overlaps the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere
It receives no energy from outside Earth
Matter is largely recycled within it
questions.explain: The biosphere depends on solar energy from outside, so it is an open system for energy.
why_wrong: This is the standard definition.
This is correct.
Nutrients cycle within the biosphere.

questions.q: A mangrove leaf in the Sundarbans photosynthesises. Which two realms exchange carbon first in this process?
questions.explain: The leaf takes carbon dioxide from air and fixes it into organic matter.
why_wrong: Carbon enters the plant from air, and rock is not the direct exchange.
Neither is the first exchange in leaf photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis in a living leaf links the atmosphere with the biosphere first.

questions.q: A flood management project needs hydrologists, economists, sociologists and lawyers. This best illustrates
options: its dependence on a single branch of biology in most cases
the multidisciplinary nature of environmental studies
its restriction to laboratory work in most cases under normal conditions
questions.explain: Environmental problems involve science, society, economics and law, so many disciplines must work together.
why_wrong: The team spans many fields.
Flood management goes beyond labs.
Law is only one of the disciplines involved.

questions.q: Which pairing of discipline and contribution to environmental studies is correct?
options: Chemistry: mapping species distribution under normal conditions
Economics: valuing costs and benefits of decisions
Law: calculating population growth rate under normal conditions
questions.explain: Economics helps price ecosystem services and weigh costs against benefits.
why_wrong: Mapping species is biology and geography.
Soil pH is measured by soil science or chemistry.
Population rates are demographic.

questions.q: A panchayat starts fining littering after a village awareness campaign. Which objective of environmental studies is served?
options: Maximising short-term industrial profit for the most part
Replacing all social sciences with natural science for the most part
Removing the need for any laws
Awareness and attitude change to protect the environment
questions.explain: Awareness leads to attitude and behaviour change.
why_wrong: This is not an objective of environmental studies.
Environmental studies is multidisciplinary.
Fines show laws remain in use.

questions.q: A councillor says technology alone can fix a city's air pollution. What is the best counterpoint?
options: Pollution has social and behavioural causes too
Technology has no role in solving environmental problems
Air pollution has only natural causes
Only governments, never citizens, can act
questions.explain: Environmental problems need policy, awareness and lifestyle change together with technology.
why_wrong: Technology helps but is not enough alone.
Human activity contributes heavily.
Citizen behaviour matters.

questions.q: A forest is protected because it has intrinsic value apart from any use to humans. Which ethical view does this reflect?
questions.explain: Ecocentrism assigns value to ecosystems and nature for their own sake.
why_wrong: This values nature only for human benefit.
It values nature only as a commodity.
It prioritises production over protection.

questions.q: A B.Tech student says EVS is only for biology majors. Which rebuttal is most appropriate?
options: Engineering never affects the environment under normal conditions
Only biologists can be affected by pollution under normal conditions
Designs affect resource use, so engineers need this knowledge
questions.explain: Engineers design systems that consume resources and create waste, so they need environmental understanding.
why_wrong: Engineered projects often affect it greatly.
Pollution affects everyone.
It includes science and social aspects.

questions.q: Which statement about the scope of environmental studies is accurate?
options: Resources, ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution and society
It is restricted to wildlife protection for the most part as a general rule
It is restricted to measuring pollution for the most part
It is restricted to climate science
questions.explain: The scope is broad, spanning resources, ecology, pollution and social dimensions.
why_wrong: It covers far more than wildlife.
Measurement is one small part.
Climate is only one topic.

questions.q: A mangrove restoration team includes a botanist, an economist and local fisherfolk who describe how the community uses the coast. Which dimension does the fisherfolk input mainly add?
options: A purely geological dimension as a general rule
A purely astronomical dimension as a general rule
questions.explain: Local communities supply knowledge of use, dependence and values, which natural science alone cannot.
why_wrong: Fisherfolk testimony is not chemical analysis.
It does not concern rock formation.
It is unrelated to astronomy.

questions.q: A council allows harvest of forest produce only at a rate that lets the forest regrow for its grandchildren. Which concept does this match?
options: Meeting present needs without harming future generations
Complete ban on resource use in most cases under normal conditions
Maximum short-term extraction in most cases under normal conditions
questions.explain: This matches the Brundtland definition.
why_wrong: It ignores future needs and resource limits.
Sustainable development allows use within limits.
It exhausts the resource for the future.

questions.q: The widely used definition of sustainable development was popularised by a UN commission chaired by whom?
questions.explain: The commission's 1987 report Our Common Future popularised the definition.
why_wrong: She wrote Silent Spring and did not chair this commission.
He led the Stockholm and Rio conferences, not this commission.
She founded the Green Belt Movement, not this commission.

questions.q: A company burns coal for most of its power but adds a small solar plant and claims to be sustainable. What is the best critique?
options: Any small solar plant makes a firm fully sustainable for the most part
Coal is non-renewable and polluting, whatever the solar share
Sustainability concerns only profit for the most part as a general rule
questions.explain: Heavy coal use depletes a finite resource and emits pollutants.
why_wrong: A token plant does not offset the main impact.
Coal takes millions of years to form.
It also concerns society and the environment.

questions.q: How does sustainability differ from sustainable development?
options: They are identical in every respect
Sustainability is the goal; sustainable development is the process
Sustainable development is the goal and sustainability is a policy as a general rule
Sustainability applies only to economics as a general rule in most cases
questions.explain: Sustainability is the end state, and sustainable development is the pathway.
why_wrong: They are related but not identical.
This reverses them.
It applies to environment and society too.

questions.q: Fishers in Kerala observe a seasonal trawling ban during the monsoon breeding season. Which principle is applied?
options: Harvesting as much as possible at all times in most cases
Harvesting no faster than the stock regenerates
Switching to non-living resources only in most cases
questions.explain: The ban lets fish stocks breed and recover.
why_wrong: This depletes stocks.
The ban exists because of breeding.
The aim is to manage renewable stocks.

questions.q: A policy compensates villagers displaced by a dam, treating today's affected poor fairly. Which equity does this represent?
questions.explain: It concerns fairness among people living in the present generation.
why_wrong: This concerns fairness between present and future generations.
This concerns fairness between species.
This is not a standard sustainability concept.

questions.q: A municipal planner refers to the global action plan for sustainable development adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Which plan is meant?
questions.explain: Agenda 21 was the action plan adopted at the 1992 Rio Summit.
why_wrong: It deals with greenhouse gas reduction, adopted in 1997.
It concerns ozone-depleting substances.
It concerns wetlands.

questions.q: A solar plant in Gujarat cuts emissions, employs local people and lowers electricity cost. Which pillars does it serve?
options: Environmental only as a general rule
Environmental and technological as a general rule
questions.explain: It reduces emissions (environmental), gives jobs (social) and saves cost (economic).
why_wrong: It also gives jobs and lowers cost.
It also reduces emissions and creates jobs.
Technological is not one of the three standard pillars.

questions.q: A profitable factory employs many workers but dumps untreated effluent in a river. Which pillar is neglected and what follows?
options: Economic; it is unprofitable in most cases under normal conditions
Environmental; the project is unsustainable in the long run
None; all three are served in most cases under normal conditions
questions.explain: Ignoring the environmental pillar degrades resources that the economy and society depend on.
why_wrong: The factory is profitable, so the economic pillar is served.
It employs many workers.
The effluent shows the environment is neglected.

questions.q: A firm's report uses the 'people, planet, profit' framework. Which pillar does 'planet' stand for?
questions.explain: Planet corresponds to the environmental pillar.
why_wrong: People corresponds to the social pillar.
Profit corresponds to the economic pillar.
It is not a standard pillar.

questions.q: In the Venn diagram of sustainability, the overlap of the environmental and economic pillars is called
questions.explain: Environmental plus economic gives viable, social plus economic gives equitable, and environmental plus social gives bearable.
why_wrong: This is environmental plus social.
This is social plus economic.
It is not a standard overlap label.

questions.q: A leather town has a clean river and strong profits but widespread child labour and no safety nets. Which pillar is weak?
questions.explain: Child labour and lack of protection indicate a weak social pillar.
why_wrong: The river is clean.
Profits are strong.
It is not a standard pillar.

questions.q: In the nested model of sustainability, how are the pillars arranged?
options: Three unrelated circles with no overlap
Economy at the centre with environment as an externality
Economy within society within the environment
questions.explain: The nested model shows dependence on the environment as the base.
why_wrong: This reverses dependence.
The nested model shows nesting.
This is not the nested model's view.

questions.q: The deer population on an island rises quickly, then levels off near a constant number. What does this plateau represent?
questions.explain: The plateau is the maximum population the environment can support.
why_wrong: This is the maximum growth rate, not the plateau.
This is the rapid growth stage.
It is not a plateau.

questions.q: Which statement about carrying capacity is correct?
options: It is fixed for all time
It changes with resources, technology and consumption
It is the same for all species for the most part as a general rule
It depends only on birth rate for the most part as a general rule
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is not fixed.
why_wrong: It varies.
It differs by species.
It depends on resources and environment.

questions.q: A Rajasthan pasture supports 100 cattle sustainably, but the owner keeps 180. What is the likely long-term outcome?
options: The pasture's carrying capacity rises as a general rule
Overgrazing degrades pasture and lowers its capacity
The cattle number can grow without limit as a general rule
questions.explain: Stocking beyond the limit damages vegetation and soil.
why_wrong: Overuse reduces capacity.
Excess grazing causes damage.
Resources are finite.

questions.q: In logistic growth, the population growth rate is highest when population size N is
options: Close to zero in most cases
Equal to K in most cases
questions.explain: Growth rate is greatest at the midpoint of the curve.
why_wrong: Growth is small.
Growth stops at K.
Population beyond K declines.

questions.q: A city consumes resources from an area ten times larger than itself, beyond what the planet regenerates. This is called
questions.explain: Overshoot means demand on nature exceeds its regenerative capacity.
why_wrong: This describes birth and death rate change.
This is the buildup of toxins along food chains.
This is the change of communities over time.

questions.q: After wolves are removed, deer on an island boom, overgraze, and then crash. Which describes this sequence?
options: It stayed below carrying capacity throughout for the most part
Carrying capacity rose permanently for the most part
It overshot K, damaged resources, then declined
questions.explain: Overshoot degrades resources and causes a crash.
why_wrong: The crash shows overshoot.
Overgrazing lowered capacity.
Removal of predators caused the boom.

questions.q: A pond holds abundant food but fish numbers are capped by low dissolved oxygen. Which principle explains this?
options: Abundant food always sets the limit
Carrying capacity is unrelated to resources as a general rule
Fish numbers are limited by food only as a general rule
A limiting factor sets K (Liebig's law of the minimum)
questions.explain: The scarcest resource limits population size.
why_wrong: Oxygen is the limiting item here.
It is determined by resources.
